reading.body:
Insurance for AI and cloud risk is splitting in two: standard carriers are excluding generative AI, while operators self-insure through captives, mutual pools and catastrophe bonds.

The pattern is a transfer of risk away from conventional insurers and back toward the parties running the compute. Generative AI exclusion endorsements and reinsurance capacity caps shrink what standard cover will absorb. Hyperscaler single parent captives, startup mutual risk pools, surplus lines and Lloyd's take what remains. Parametric micro-insurance on API and GPU availability turns uptime itself into a priced exposure, and catastrophe bonds extend the same logic to multi-day cloud shutdowns.

This matters for AI because it makes failure a financial instrument rather than an operational accident. If a multi-day outage can be hedged and model performance can be backed by a policy, then the cost of unreliability enters the balance sheet alongside the cost of power and silicon. Certification-linked discounts go further, tying the price of cover to whether an enterprise passes a third party safety audit, which converts governance from a compliance exercise into a line item.

What the material does not supply is scale. There are no premiums, no capacity figures, no named carriers, no dates and no indication of how much risk has actually moved into these structures. It is a map of mechanisms, not a measurement of the market, and it cannot say whether any of them is large or marginal.
